items.prompt: In CAP theorem, what does the "A" (Availability) actually promise?
choices: Every request that reaches a working node gets a response, rather than an error
Every replica always holds the exact same data at every instant
The system never loses a network packet
Every write is saved permanently, even across a crash
items.explanation: Availability is specifically about a working node always answering a request — it says nothing about whether that answer is the freshest possible value, which is Consistency's job instead.
items.reference:
C — same answer everywhere
A — always answers
P — survives dropped/delayed messages

Why: the bank Scenario's Datacenter B had to trade one of these against another the instant the network link died.

items.prompt: What does the "C" (Consistency) in CAP theorem promise?
choices: Every node returns the same, most-recent value for a given piece of data
The system stores data on disk instead of only in memory
Every request is answered within a fixed time budget
Data is encrypted the same way on every node
items.explanation: CAP's Consistency is about agreement on the current value across nodes — not about durability, latency, or encryption, which are separate concerns entirely.
items.reference:
C — same answer everywhere
A — always answers
P — survives dropped/delayed messages

Why: the bank Scenario's Datacenter B had to trade one of these against another the instant the network link died.

items.prompt: What does "Partition tolerance" (P) in CAP theorem describe?
choices: The system keeps working even when network messages between nodes are lost or delayed
The database splits large tables into smaller physical partitions for performance
Every node is deployed in a different geographic region
The system tolerates a fixed number of corrupted records
items.explanation: Partition tolerance is about surviving broken communication between nodes — not table sharding for performance, which is an unrelated database design choice with the same word.
items.reference:
C — same answer everywhere
A — always answers
P — survives dropped/delayed messages

Why: the bank Scenario's Datacenter B had to trade one of these against another the instant the network link died.

items.prompt: "Pick any two of C, A, P" is a common summary of CAP theorem. What's misleading about it?
choices: Partitions will happen on any real network, so P isn't something you can simply opt out of — the real choice is only between C and A, and only during a partition
It's wrong because you can actually have all three at once, all the time
It's misleading because CAP theorem has four properties, not three
It's misleading because Availability and Consistency mean the same thing
items.explanation: Networks drop packets and links get cut in the real world, so partition tolerance isn't optional the way the mnemonic implies — the actual, narrower choice CAP forces is between C and A, and only while a partition is actually happening.
items.reference:
Outside a partition: a healthy system can offer both C and A. During a partition: only one survives per request.

Why: real networks fail, so 'don't pick P' isn't an available option — the interesting trade-off only shows up when P is forced on you.

items.prompt: A system runs with a perfectly healthy network between all its nodes, no dropped or delayed messages. According to CAP theorem, can it offer both Consistency and Availability at the same time?
choices: Yes — CAP's trade-off only forces a choice specifically while a partition is happening
No — CAP theorem says you must always sacrifice one of the three, network health or not
Yes, but only if it has exactly one node
No — a healthy network actually makes the trade-off worse
items.explanation: CAP's impossibility result is specifically about what happens during a partition — with the network fully healthy, a well-built system can offer both Consistency and Availability simultaneously.
items.reference:
Outside a partition: a healthy system can offer both C and A. During a partition: only one survives per request.

Why: real networks fail, so 'don't pick P' isn't an available option — the interesting trade-off only shows up when P is forced on you.

items.prompt: In the bank Scenario, Datacenter B is cut off from A and gets a withdrawal request. What are its only two real options?
choices: Approve the withdrawal without confirming with A (favoring Availability), or refuse to answer until the link returns (favoring Consistency)
Approve the withdrawal only for amounts under $100, or approve all withdrawals equally
Ask the customer to come back tomorrow, or automatically transfer them to Datacenter A
Approve every request and let Datacenter A silently overwrite any conflict later, with no other option available
items.explanation: With no way to confirm A's current state, B genuinely has just two options: answer anyway (risking a wrong answer, favoring Availability) or refuse to answer at all (favoring Consistency) — no third option gives a fast, guaranteed-correct answer during the outage.
items.reference:
Cut off from A, B must choose per request: answer (maybe wrong) or refuse (definitely safe, but no service).

Why: this is CAP's real, narrow choice — not a menu of three options, exactly two, and only while the partition lasts.

items.prompt: If Datacenter B refuses to answer the withdrawal request until the network link to A is restored, which property is it prioritizing?
choices: Consistency — it will not risk giving a possibly-wrong answer, even at the cost of serving no answer at all
Availability — refusing to answer is itself a form of high availability
Partition tolerance — refusing requests is how a system tolerates partitions
Durability — refusing protects the durability of the stored balance
items.explanation: Refusing to answer until the link is safely restored is choosing correctness over responsiveness — that's prioritizing Consistency, at the direct cost of Availability for that request.
items.reference:
Cut off from A, B must choose per request: answer (maybe wrong) or refuse (definitely safe, but no service).

Why: this is CAP's real, narrow choice — not a menu of three options, exactly two, and only while the partition lasts.

items.prompt: Out of the box, which of these systems typically leans CP (stops a minority partition from accepting writes rather than risk disagreement)?
choices: Zookeeper / etcd
Cassandra with default settings
DynamoDB with default settings
Riak with default settings
items.explanation: Zookeeper and etcd are coordination services built around a strict, agreed-upon single history — a minority side of a partition deliberately stops serving writes rather than risk two histories diverging.
items.reference:
CP-leaningZookeeper, etcd, CockroachDB
AP-leaningCassandra, DynamoDB, Riak (defaults)

Why: the lean is a default, not a permanent label — most of these systems let you tune it per request via the quorum settings covered in L2.

items.prompt: Out of the box, which of these systems typically leans AP (every reachable replica keeps answering during a partition, resolving conflicts later)?
choices: Cassandra with default settings
Zookeeper
etcd
CockroachDB
items.explanation: Cassandra's default posture keeps every reachable replica serving reads and writes during a partition, reconciling any conflicting writes afterward — the classic AP lean.
items.reference:
CP-leaningZookeeper, etcd, CockroachDB
AP-leaningCassandra, DynamoDB, Riak (defaults)

Why: the lean is a default, not a permanent label — most of these systems let you tune it per request via the quorum settings covered in L2.

items.prompt: CockroachDB and Spanner-style systems typically lean which direction, and why?
choices: CP — they sacrifice availability on a minority partition to keep a single consistent history
AP — they always keep every replica answering, no matter what
Neither — CAP theorem doesn't apply to SQL-style databases
AP, because they use SQL instead of a key-value model
items.explanation: CockroachDB and Spanner-style systems are built to keep a single, globally-consistent history — they'll refuse writes on a minority partition rather than risk two versions of the truth diverging.
items.reference:
CP-leaningZookeeper, etcd, CockroachDB
AP-leaningCassandra, DynamoDB, Riak (defaults)

Why: the lean is a default, not a permanent label — most of these systems let you tune it per request via the quorum settings covered in L2.

items.prompt: A team chooses to make their withdrawal service AP-leaning during partitions, always approving requests on both sides. What's the realistic consequence, using the bank Scenario's numbers?
choices: An account can go negative if both sides approve withdrawals against the same balance before the partition heals
Customers will simply see slightly different UI colors on each side
The system will refuse every withdrawal until the partition heals
Nothing changes — AP and CP behave identically for money
items.explanation: Choosing Availability during a partition means both sides keep approving requests without confirming with each other — for a shared balance, that can really let the account go negative, exactly like the Scenario describes.
items.reference:
Choosing A during a partition: fast answers, risk of a wrong one (e.g. double-spend). Choosing C: guaranteed-correct, risk of no answer at all.

Why: the 'right' choice depends on which failure mode the business can tolerate less — there's no universally correct pick.

items.prompt: A team instead chooses to make their withdrawal service CP-leaning, refusing requests on any side that can't confirm with the others. What's the realistic consequence during a real partition?
choices: Legitimate customers on the cut-off side get "service unavailable" until connectivity returns, even though their local balance data isn't actually corrupted
The account can silently go negative
Nothing changes — CP and AP behave identically for money
Only withdrawals over $1,000 are affected
items.explanation: Choosing Consistency during a partition means refusing to answer rather than risk being wrong — the real cost is availability: working customers on the cut-off side get no service until the network is restored.
items.reference:
Choosing A during a partition: fast answers, risk of a wrong one (e.g. double-spend). Choosing C: guaranteed-correct, risk of no answer at all.

Why: the 'right' choice depends on which failure mode the business can tolerate less — there's no universally correct pick.

items.prompt: A social media "like" counter briefly shows slightly different counts to two users at the same instant, then converges. Which consistency model is this a textbook fit for?
choices: Eventual consistency
Strong (linearizable) consistency
Read-your-writes
Causal consistency
items.explanation: A like counter tolerates brief disagreement as long as it eventually converges, with no promise about exactly when — the cheapest model that matches this requirement is eventual consistency, not a stronger (and more expensive) guarantee the use case doesn't need.
items.reference:
Strongalways freshest, everywhere, instantly
Causalpreserves cause-before-effect order
Read-your-writesyou always see your own prior writes
Eventualconverges, no promise on timing

Why: picking the weakest model that actually satisfies the requirement avoids paying for coordination the use case never needed.

items.prompt: A banking withdrawal needs every read, everywhere, to reflect the single most recent completed write — instantly, with no exceptions. Which model does that describe?
choices: Strong (linearizable) consistency
Eventual consistency
Read-your-writes
None of these models can express that requirement
items.explanation: "Most recent write, everywhere, instantly, no exceptions" is the definition of strong (linearizable) consistency — the strictest, and most expensive, point on the spectrum.
items.reference:
Strongalways freshest, everywhere, instantly
Causalpreserves cause-before-effect order
Read-your-writesyou always see your own prior writes
Eventualconverges, no promise on timing

Why: picking the weakest model that actually satisfies the requirement avoids paying for coordination the use case never needed.

items.prompt: A comment thread guarantees that if reply B was written after seeing comment A, every reader sees A before B — but two unrelated comments posted around the same time might show in either order for different readers. Which model is this?
choices: Causal consistency
Strong consistency
Eventual consistency with no guarantees at all
Read-your-writes
items.explanation: Preserving order only for writes that are actually causally related (a reply that depended on seeing the original) while leaving unrelated writes' relative order unspecified is exactly causal consistency — cheaper than strong, stronger than plain eventual.
items.reference:
Strongalways freshest, everywhere, instantly
Causalpreserves cause-before-effect order
Read-your-writesyou always see your own prior writes
Eventualconverges, no promise on timing

Why: picking the weakest model that actually satisfies the requirement avoids paying for coordination the use case never needed.

items.prompt: What is the defining cost of strong (linearizable) consistency compared to weaker models?
choices: Every read or write may need to coordinate across nodes before it can complete, since it must reflect the single latest state system-wide
It requires more disk space per replica
It only works with exactly 2 replicas
It cannot be combined with replication at all
items.explanation: Guaranteeing every read sees the absolute latest write system-wide, instantly, requires coordination between nodes on the hot path of a request — that coordination is what makes strong consistency the most expensive point on the spectrum.
items.reference:
Strong consistency's promise (always-freshest, everywhere) is exactly why it's the most expensive: the guarantee has to be re-earned on every single operation.

Why: a model's cost tracks how much coordination its guarantee requires — not an arbitrary label.

items.prompt: Why is eventual consistency cheaper to operate than strong consistency?
choices: Writes and reads never have to wait on each other to coordinate — they proceed independently and the system converges later
It uses less encryption
It only stores a single copy of the data
It's cheaper because it never allows any writes to fail
items.explanation: Eventual consistency's cheapness comes directly from not requiring coordination on the read/write hot path — replicas update independently and are simply promised to converge eventually, with no promise about exactly when.
items.reference:
Strong consistency's promise (always-freshest, everywhere) is exactly why it's the most expensive: the guarantee has to be re-earned on every single operation.

Why: a model's cost tracks how much coordination its guarantee requires — not an arbitrary label.

items.prompt: With N=5 replicas, W=3, R=3, is a read guaranteed to see the latest acknowledged write?
choices: Yes — W + R = 6 > N = 5, so the write and read sets must overlap by at least one replica
No — W and R would both need to equal N
No — quorum guarantees only apply when N is even
Yes, but only if W equals R exactly
items.explanation: The formula only requires W + R > N. Here 3 + 3 = 6, which is greater than 5, so any W-sized write set and R-sized read set drawn from the same 5 replicas must share at least one replica — the overlap guarantee holds.
items.reference:
W + R > N guarantees a write set and a read set drawn from N replicas must overlap.

Why: this is pigeonhole reasoning, not a database-specific rule — it holds for any N, W, R satisfying the inequality.

items.prompt: With N=4 replicas, W=2, R=2, is a read guaranteed to see the latest acknowledged write?
choices: No — W + R = 4, which is not greater than N = 4, so a write set and read set could be chosen with zero overlap
Yes — W + R equals N, which is always sufficient
Yes, because W equals R
No, because N is even
items.explanation: The formula requires a strict W + R > N, not W + R >= N. With 2 + 2 = 4 = N, it's possible to pick 2 replicas for the write and a completely different 2 for the read out of the same 4, with no shared replica — the guarantee does not hold.
items.reference:
W + R > N guarantees a write set and a read set drawn from N replicas must overlap.

Why: this is pigeonhole reasoning, not a database-specific rule — it holds for any N, W, R satisfying the inequality.

items.prompt: Why does W + R > N guarantee overlap between a write set and a read set, rather than just making it likely?
choices: It's a pigeonhole argument: you cannot choose a W-sized set and an R-sized set from only N items without them sharing at least one item once their sizes sum past N
It's a statistical guarantee that only holds on average over many requests
It's guaranteed only because most databases use random replica selection
It isn't actually guaranteed — it's just a strong heuristic
items.explanation: This is deterministic pigeonhole reasoning, not a probability: with a pool of only N replicas, a set of size W and a set of size R whose sizes sum to more than N cannot be chosen disjointly — they must share at least one member.
items.reference:
W + R > N guarantees a write set and a read set drawn from N replicas must overlap.

Why: this is pigeonhole reasoning, not a database-specific rule — it holds for any N, W, R satisfying the inequality.

items.prompt: A team sets W=1 (write to just 1 of N replicas is enough to succeed) to make writes as fast as possible. What do they give up?
choices: The overlap guarantee — reads are no longer guaranteed to see the latest write unless R is set very high to compensate
Nothing — W=1 has no consequences as long as R is also 1
Durability of the data already written
The ability to ever read the data again
items.explanation: A tiny W makes writes cheap and fast, but shrinks how many replicas are guaranteed to hold the new value — unless R is raised enough to compensate (W + R > N), reads risk landing on a replica that never got the write.
items.reference:
W=1, R=1fastest, no overlap guarantee
W=N, R=1slow writes, always-fresh reads
majority/majoritybalanced, overlap guaranteed

Why: W and R aren't independent knobs — raising one can compensate for lowering the other, as long as their sum still exceeds N.

items.prompt: A team sets W=N (every single replica must ack a write). What's the operational risk this introduces?
choices: Any single unreachable replica blocks every write, even if the rest of the cluster is perfectly healthy
Reads become slower than writes
The overlap guarantee is lost
Data can be silently lost on every write
items.explanation: Requiring every replica to ack means the write's success now depends on the least available replica in the cluster — a single slow or unreachable node blocks every write, which is a severe availability cost for guaranteed-fresh reads in return.
items.reference:
W=1, R=1fastest, no overlap guarantee
W=N, R=1slow writes, always-fresh reads
majority/majoritybalanced, overlap guaranteed

Why: W and R aren't independent knobs — raising one can compensate for lowering the other, as long as their sum still exceeds N.

items.prompt: A user posts a comment, then immediately refreshes their own feed and expects to see it there right away, even before it's replicated everywhere. Which model is the minimum needed to guarantee that?
choices: Read-your-writes
Strong (linearizable) consistency
Eventual consistency
Causal consistency
items.explanation: Read-your-writes specifically promises a client sees its own prior writes — that's exactly this requirement, and it's cheaper than reaching for full strong consistency to guarantee a global property the use case never asked for.
items.reference:
Read-your-writes only tracks one client's own session — it says nothing about what other clients see or when.

Why: matching the requirement to the cheapest sufficient model avoids over-paying for coordination other clients don't need.

items.prompt: Read-your-writes guarantees a client sees its own prior writes. What does it NOT promise?
choices: That any other client sees that write, or sees it in any particular order relative to other writes
That the client's own writes are ever saved at all
That the client can read any data whatsoever
That the write eventually reaches any other replica
items.explanation: Read-your-writes is a purely per-client guarantee — it says nothing about when, or in what order, other clients see that same write, which is what a stronger model like causal or strong consistency would need to promise instead.
items.reference:
Read-your-writes only tracks one client's own session — it says nothing about what other clients see or when.

Why: matching the requirement to the cheapest sufficient model avoids over-paying for coordination other clients don't need.

items.prompt: Why is read-your-writes cheaper to implement than full causal consistency?
choices: It only needs to track one client's own session/writes, rather than the causal ordering between every write in the system
It doesn't require any replication at all
It's implemented entirely on the client with no server support
It only applies to read-only systems
items.explanation: Read-your-writes can be implemented by routing a client's own subsequent reads to a replica known to have its own recent writes (or tracking a per-session version) — far cheaper than tracking causal relationships between every write across every client, which is what full causal consistency requires.
items.reference:
Read-your-writes only tracks one client's own session — it says nothing about what other clients see or when.

Why: matching the requirement to the cheapest sufficient model avoids over-paying for coordination other clients don't need.

items.prompt: Implement `quorumWrite(reachableCount, w)` which returns `true` if a write succeeds given how many replicas are currently reachable and the required write quorum `w`. A write succeeds only if at least `w` reachable replicas can be written to.
items.explanation: A quorum write's success is purely a comparison: it succeeds exactly when the number of replicas it could actually reach meets or exceeds the required write quorum w — no partial credit, no averaging.
items.reference:
A write only reports success once w replicas ack — fewer reachable replicas than w means the write must report failure, even if some replicas were still updated.

Why: ignoring the returned success flag is exactly the bug class from L1's bank example.

items.prompt: Implement `ackedCount(replicas)` which takes an array of `{ reachable: boolean }` objects and returns how many of them are reachable (i.e. would ack a write).
items.explanation: Counting acks is a straightforward filter over the reachable flag — this count is exactly what a real quorumWrite compares against w to decide whether to report success.
items.reference:
A write only reports success once w replicas ack — fewer reachable replicas than w means the write must report failure, even if some replicas were still updated.

Why: ignoring the returned success flag is exactly the bug class from L1's bank example.

items.prompt: Implement `writeSucceeds(n, unreachableIds, targetIds, w)` — given total replicas `n`, a list of currently unreachable replica ids, a list of replica ids the write targets, and quorum `w`, return true if enough targeted replicas are reachable to satisfy the quorum.

tests.description: one target unreachable, still meets lower quorum

items.explanation: Only targeted replicas that are also currently reachable count toward the quorum — filtering out any target id present in the unreachable list, then comparing the remaining count to w, mirrors exactly what a real quorum write does during a partition.
items.reference:
A write only reports success once w replicas ack — fewer reachable replicas than w means the write must report failure, even if some replicas were still updated.

Why: ignoring the returned success flag is exactly the bug class from L1's bank example.

items.prompt: Implement `latestValue(responses)` — given an array of `{ value, timestamp }` objects returned by a quorum read, return the `value` from the response with the highest `timestamp` (last-write-wins).
items.explanation: Last-write-wins resolves a set of quorum-read responses by taking the one with the largest timestamp — the reduce compares every response pairwise and keeps whichever is newer, regardless of the order they arrived in.
items.reference:
With W + R > N, at least one of the R responses is guaranteed to be the newest acknowledged write — last-write-wins just has to find it.

Why: without the quorum overlap guarantee, picking 'the highest timestamp among R responses' would just be guessing, not proving freshness.

items.prompt: Implement `hasOverlap(n, w, r)` — return true if a write quorum `w` and read quorum `r` out of `n` total replicas are guaranteed to overlap by at least one replica.

tests.description: equal to n is not enough (strict inequality)

items.explanation: The quorum overlap guarantee is a strict inequality, W + R > N — W + R equal to N is not enough, since a write set and a read set of those sizes could still be chosen with zero shared replicas out of exactly N.
items.reference:
With W + R > N, at least one of the R responses is guaranteed to be the newest acknowledged write — last-write-wins just has to find it.

Why: without the quorum overlap guarantee, picking 'the highest timestamp among R responses' would just be guessing, not proving freshness.

items.prompt: Implement `resolveRead(responses)` — given an array of `{ value, timestamp }` (possibly empty, meaning no replica had the key), return the freshest `{ value, timestamp }` object, or `undefined` if the array is empty.
items.explanation: The empty-responses case (no queried replica had the key at all, e.g. a key that was never written or a replica set that's entirely down) has to be handled explicitly before reducing — reduce with no initial value throws on an empty array, and undefined is the honest signal that no data was found, not a fabricated default.
items.reference:
With W + R > N, at least one of the R responses is guaranteed to be the newest acknowledged write — last-write-wins just has to find it.

Why: without the quorum overlap guarantee, picking 'the highest timestamp among R responses' would just be guessing, not proving freshness.

items.prompt: Implement `resolveConflict(a, b)` where `a` and `b` are `{ value, timestamp }` writes to the same key. Return whichever has the higher timestamp. If timestamps are exactly equal, return `a` (a fixed, deterministic tiebreak).
items.explanation: Last-write-wins compares timestamps and keeps the larger one; a deterministic tiebreak (favoring a on an exact tie) matters because without one, two replicas resolving the same tie independently could disagree and never converge.
items.reference:
LWW picks a winner by timestamp — it doesn't detect that both writes were 'real', it just discards the loser.

Why: a timestamp tiebreak has to be deterministic across replicas, or two nodes could each 'win' the same tie differently and never agree.

items.prompt: Implement `mergeReplicaViews(views)` — given an array of `{ value, timestamp }` writes seen across multiple replicas for the same key, return the single last-write-wins result across all of them (highest timestamp; on a tie, prefer the item appearing earlier in the array).
items.explanation: reduce with a strict greater-than comparison naturally keeps the earliest entry on a tie, since a later equal-timestamp entry never satisfies `>` against the current winner — the same LWW rule scales from two writes to any number of replica views.
items.reference:
LWW picks a winner by timestamp — it doesn't detect that both writes were 'real', it just discards the loser.

Why: a timestamp tiebreak has to be deterministic across replicas, or two nodes could each 'win' the same tie differently and never agree.

items.prompt: Implement `wasOverwritten(candidate, winner)` — given a candidate write and the LWW winner for the same key, return true if the candidate's value was silently discarded (i.e. candidate is not the winner and has a strictly lower timestamp).

tests.description: equal timestamp, different write, not strictly lower -> not overwritten by this definition

items.explanation: A write counts as silently overwritten only when it has a strictly lower timestamp than the winner — this makes visible exactly what last-write-wins discards without any special-casing, which is the concrete cost the L3 Checkpoint discusses (a real, valid write can vanish from every future read).
items.reference:
LWW picks a winner by timestamp — it doesn't detect that both writes were 'real', it just discards the loser.

Why: a timestamp tiebreak has to be deterministic across replicas, or two nodes could each 'win' the same tie differently and never agree.

items.prompt: Implement `isReadGuaranteedFresh(n, w, r)` — return true only if the read quorum r, combined with the write quorum w, is guaranteed to see the latest write out of n total replicas.
items.explanation: Freshness of a read is exactly the quorum overlap condition from L2 — w + r > n — restated as a yes/no check; this is the same formula as hasOverlap, applied to the specific question of whether a read is guaranteed current.
items.reference:
Shrinking R to make reads cheap only stays safe if W grows enough to keep W + R > N — otherwise the read is no longer guaranteed fresh.

Why: a 'fast read' setting that silently drops the freshness guarantee is a correctness bug waiting to be discovered in production, not a free optimization.

items.prompt: Implement `minReadQuorumFor(n, w)` — given n total replicas and a fixed write quorum w, return the minimum r needed to guarantee read freshness (smallest integer r such that w + r > n).
items.explanation: Solving w + r > n for the smallest integer r gives r = n - w + 1 — one more than the largest r that would fail the strict inequality (n - w), which is exactly why write-everywhere (w=n) only needs a single-replica read (r=1) to be guaranteed fresh.
items.reference:
Shrinking R to make reads cheap only stays safe if W grows enough to keep W + R > N — otherwise the read is no longer guaranteed fresh.

Why: a 'fast read' setting that silently drops the freshness guarantee is a correctness bug waiting to be discovered in production, not a free optimization.

items.prompt: Implement `canReachQuorum(sideSize, w)` — given how many replicas are on one side of a network partition and a required write quorum w, return true if that side alone can still satisfy w.
items.explanation: Whether a side of a partition can keep accepting writes comes down to whether it alone has at least w replicas — with a majority-sized w, only one side of any partition can ever satisfy it at a time, which is exactly what stops both sides from accepting conflicting writes simultaneously under CP settings.
items.reference:
With a majority write quorum, at most one side of any partition can reach it — the other side is forced to refuse writes (CP behavior).

Why: this is the concrete mechanism behind L1's 'only one side survives' rule — it falls out of simple arithmetic on quorum size, not a special partition-detection algorithm.

items.prompt: Implement `bothSidesCanWrite(sideA, sideB, w)` — given the replica counts on both sides of a partition and a write quorum w, return true if BOTH sides could independently satisfy the quorum (a dangerous split-brain condition).

tests.description: majority quorum: only one side can ever qualify
low quorum: both sides can qualify (split-brain risk)

items.explanation: Split-brain — both sides of a partition independently accepting writes — is only possible if w is small enough that both sides can each reach it on their own; setting w to a strict majority of n makes this impossible, since two disjoint sides of the same n replicas can't both hold a majority.
items.reference:
With a majority write quorum, at most one side of any partition can reach it — the other side is forced to refuse writes (CP behavior).

Why: this is the concrete mechanism behind L1's 'only one side survives' rule — it falls out of simple arithmetic on quorum size, not a special partition-detection algorithm.

items.prompt: Implement `majorityQuorum(n)` — return the smallest write quorum w that guarantees only one side of any network partition can ever satisfy it (a strict majority of n).
items.explanation: A strict majority of n is floor(n/2) + 1 — for both odd n (3 -> 2, 5 -> 3) and even n (4 -> 3), this is the smallest integer that no two disjoint subsets of n replicas can both reach, which is exactly the property that prevents split-brain writes on both sides of a partition at once.
items.reference:
With a majority write quorum, at most one side of any partition can reach it — the other side is forced to refuse writes (CP behavior).

Why: this is the concrete mechanism behind L1's 'only one side survives' rule — it falls out of simple arithmetic on quorum size, not a special partition-detection algorithm.
